name: Social and Emotional Wellbeing
what: This subtopic covers social wellbeing, defined as the ability to form and maintain meaningful bonds and adapt to social situations, and emotional wellbeing, defined as the ability to control and express emotions adaptively and understand others' emotions. It examines how these two dimensions are distinct but deeply interconnected.
why: Social and emotional wellbeing are central to everyday functioning and are frequently tested in VCE exam scenarios. Understanding both separately and together prepares students for analysis tasks.

items.title: I can define social wellbeing
items.what: Social wellbeing is the ability for an individual to form and maintain meaningful bonds with others, and to adapt to different social situations. It includes having a strong support network and being able to communicate effectively.
items.why: This is an assessable definition. Exam questions may ask students to identify or explain social wellbeing using evidence from a scenario, so precise knowledge of the definition is necessary.
items.example: Tina, after joining an English class and a netball team, develops friendships, communicates more effectively with colleagues, and builds a local support network. These outcomes reflect improved social wellbeing.

items.title: I can describe characteristics of high and low social wellbeing
items.what: High social wellbeing involves having a strong support network, forming and maintaining meaningful relationships, and communicating effectively. Low social wellbeing involves isolation, difficulty forming relationships, and poor communication with others.
items.why: Describing the two ends of social wellbeing with specific markers allows students to match scenario evidence to the correct level of social wellbeing in analysis questions.
items.example: Tom, after losing his job, maintained contact with former colleagues and relied on two close friends for help moving house. Despite his circumstances, this reflects high social wellbeing.

items.title: I can define emotional wellbeing
items.what: Emotional wellbeing is the ability to appropriately control and express one's own emotions in an adaptive way, and to understand and respond to the emotions of others. It includes experiencing a wide range of emotions while expressing them at suitable times.
items.why: Emotional wellbeing is a distinct but related construct to social wellbeing. Confusing the two is a common error. Knowing the definition precisely allows for accurate and differentiated exam answers.
items.example: A person who feels angry during a workplace conflict but waits until a private meeting to raise the issue calmly, rather than reacting immediately, is demonstrating high emotional wellbeing through adaptive emotion regulation.

items.title: I can describe characteristics of high and low emotional wellbeing
items.what: High emotional wellbeing involves awareness of one's own and others' emotional states, experiencing a wide range of emotions, and expressing them appropriately. Low emotional wellbeing involves difficulty naming emotions, emotional numbness, or expressing emotions at inappropriate times.
items.why: These characteristics appear in exam scenarios. Students must identify whether a character is showing high or low emotional wellbeing and justify their answer with specific evidence.
items.example: Jimmy, after amygdala damage, showed less respect for colleagues and withdrew from family. His inability to regulate and express emotions appropriately reflects low emotional wellbeing.

items.title: I can explain why social and emotional wellbeing are interrelated
items.what: Social and emotional wellbeing reinforce each other. The ability to understand and label one's own emotions enables communication of needs to others, strengthening relationships and social wellbeing. Conversely, empathy and understanding others' emotions supports the formation of meaningful relationships.
items.why: Questions often ask students to discuss social and emotional wellbeing together or to explain the connection between them. Understanding the mutual relationship between them enables more sophisticated responses.
items.example: A student who recognises that a friend seems upset (emotional awareness) and reaches out to check in (social behaviour) is demonstrating how emotional wellbeing supports social wellbeing in practice.
